evidence.title: Improving Nurses' Management of Uterine Tachysystole
evidence.venue: MCN. The American journal of maternal child nursing
evidence.outcome: Timely evidence-based nurse management of tachysystole after education added to AI alerts
evidence.effect: Significant improvement in timely management with Category II/III FHR pattern (p < .001); no change in tachysystole incidence (p = .945) or prolonged alerts (p = .377); only 31.4% of nurses completed module.
evidence.quote: Phase II found a significant improvement in the timely management of tachysystole with evidence-based intervention in the presence of Category II/III fetal heart rate pattern ( p < .001).

evidence.title: The "DeepSeek effect" and the adoption-integration gap of generative artificial intelligence in clinical practice: a national online convenience cross-sectional survey of academic critical care physicians in China

evidence.title: Integrating Generative AI Into Clinical Reasoning Education for Medical Students: Mixed Methods Study
evidence.effect: Self-perceived AI literacy improved across all domains (d=0.69-0.93, p<.001) and collaborative learning attitudes increased substantially (d=0.94, p<.001).
evidence.quote: Self-perceived AI literacy improved across all domains (Cohen d=0.69-0.93, all P<.001; all remaining significant after false discovery rate correction), and collaborative learning attitudes increased substantially (d=0.94, P<.001).

commentary.bottom_line: Three studies of user training for AI outputs report gains in nurse response timeliness, physician skill priorities, and student self-rated AI literacy, but none randomized users or followed a concurrent control group, and none measured whether trained users caught erroneous outputs. The evidence suggests training may change some behaviors and attitudes, while its effect on acceptance of wrong AI outputs remains untested.

perspectives.view: Two studies are pre-post designs without comparators. The third compared physicians with and without structured training at one time point (86.7% vs 28.6% prioritizing integration skills), and self-selection may explain that difference. No outcome measured detection of false-positive or false-negative outputs. Certainty is very low after downgrading for risk of bias and indirectness.

In the labor unit study, timely management of Category II/III fetal heart rate patterns improved after education (p < .001), but tachysystole incidence did not change (p = .945). No study tested whether training helps users recognize and override an incorrect alert, which is the failure mode this recommendation targets.

The 66 nurses who completed the module represented 31.4% of labor nurses in a real deployment. That uptake suggests training delivered alongside alerts may reach a minority of users, which makes the observed improvement hard to attribute to the module. The student study was simulated and self-reported, so its transfer to clinical workflows is unknown.

The studies took place in China, Taiwan, and one setting with no reported country. None described patient populations by insurance, language, or literacy. One endorsing source calls for teaching users whether an AI tool was trained for particular demographics, but no study tested a training component on bias.

None of the studies reported the cost, staff time, or scheduling required to deliver training. The 31.4% completion rate among nurses suggests that voluntary modules may not achieve coverage without protected time or other adoption supports. The studies do not tell leaders what those supports would cost.

commentary.research_gap: No study has randomized users or followed a concurrent control group to test whether training reduces acceptance of erroneous AI outputs, measured with seeded false-positive and false-negative cases or with audited real-world overrides. No study has linked training to patient outcomes, measured how long the effects last, or reported the cost of delivery.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the three studies reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and all enrolled clinicians or students without describing the patients they serve. Whether training helps users detect AI errors that affect these populations remains unknown.
